prompt: A raw landing table has no date column anybody trusts. Which kind of partitioning suits it?
hint: The only certain date is when the row arrived.

choices.text: By ingestion time
choices.why: Right. `_PARTITIONTIME` and `_PARTITIONDATE` hold the moment of arrival.

choices.text: By integer range on its row number
choices.why: A row number says nothing a query filters on.

choices.text: By a `DATE` column filled with today's date by the reader
choices.why: That is ingestion time done by hand, and wrong for every reader on a different day.

choices.text: None: a table without a date cannot be partitioned
choices.why: Ingestion time and integer range need no date column.

prompt: Why is ingestion-time partitioning wrong for Quitanda's orders?
hint: Think of an order that arrives a day late.

choices.text: It costs more to store
choices.why: Storage is priced the same whatever the partitioning.

choices.text: It files late orders by load day
choices.why: Right. A report on a day would then miss it.

choices.text: It cannot be filtered in a `WHERE`
choices.why: `_PARTITIONDATE` is filtered like any column.

choices.text: BigQuery limits it to hourly partitions
choices.why: Ingestion time can be cut by day and other units too.

prompt: Match each special partition to the rows it holds.
hint: One right-hand option is not a partition at all.

pairs.right: Rows whose partitioning column is null
Rows whose integer falls outside the declared range
A pseudo-column holding when an ingestion-time row arrived

right_distractors: Rows older than the partition expiration

prompt: `partition_expiration_days = 1095` removes a day of orders on its third birthday. What does that deletion cost?
hint: The pricing page lists free operations.

choices.text: Nothing
choices.why: Right. Deleting individual table partitions is free.

choices.text: A query over the partition, at 11.25 USD per TiB
choices.why: Expiration runs no query and bills no bytes.

choices.text: The 10 MB minimum, once a day
choices.why: The minimum applies to queries, and this is not one.

choices.text: One slot-minute
choices.why: No slots are billed for it.

prompt: A table is partitioned by `dt`. Which filter prunes its partitions?
hint: Keep the column alone, compared with constants.

choices.why: It names another column; the partitions are cut by `dt`.

choices.text: `dt + INTERVAL 1 DAY = DATE '2026-09-30'`
choices.why: The column is inside an expression.
Right. One file of sixty in DuckDB.

choices.text: `dt = (SELECT max(dt) FROM orders)`
choices.why: Not a constant: the day is only known after a read.

prompt: A table is partitioned by day and holds 90 days of equal size. A query reads one column for 9 of them. What fraction of the unpartitioned bill does it pay? Give a decimal.
hint: The saving is the share of partitions pruned; ignore the minimum.

prompt: `require_partition_filter` is on, and a query says `WHERE dt > DATE '2000-01-01'`. What happens?
hint: The option checks that the filter exists, not what it prunes.

choices.text: It is refused, because the filter prunes nothing
choices.why: The option does not judge how much a filter prunes.

choices.text: It runs and reads every partition
choices.why: Right. The guardrail asks for a filter, not a good one.

choices.text: It runs on the newest 90 days only
choices.why: Nothing narrows a filter by itself.

choices.text: It fails, and costs the 10 MB minimum
choices.why: It does not fail, and a failed query would cost nothing.

prompt: DuckDB pruned `strftime(dt, '%Y-%m') = '2026-09'` to 29 files. Why does this lesson still advise writing `dt BETWEEN` in BigQuery?
hint: One engine was measured; the other was documented.

choices.text: `strftime` does not exist in GoogleSQL, so the query would fail outright
choices.why: GoogleSQL has its own formatting functions; the point is the column inside one.

choices.text: Google promises pruning only for the bare column
choices.why: Right. What DuckDB does is not evidence of what BigQuery does.

choices.text: `BETWEEN` is cheaper per byte
choices.why: Every byte costs the same; the question is how many are read.

choices.text: DuckDB was wrong and read all 60 files
choices.why: The plan said 29 of 60, and that is what it opened.

prompt: The hourly layout holds the same rows as the daily one. Why was the sum per district slower on it?
hint: Count the files.

choices.text: It reads more bytes per row, since the hour is a column
choices.why: The columns and their sizes are the same.

choices.text: It opens sixteen times as many files
choices.why: Right. A fixed cost per piece, paid nearly a thousand times.

choices.text: Its files are compressed harder
choices.why: The sizes came out about the same.

choices.text: DuckDB skips hourly partitions
choices.why: It read all of them; this query has no filter.

prompt: Quitanda's evening-rush report asks about 18:00 to 21:00 of a day. What does this lesson suggest for it?
hint: Partition by the coarsest unit the common filters still prune well.

choices.text: Partition by hour instead of by day
choices.why: That multiplies the partitions for every other query.

choices.text: Keep daily partitions and cluster on the hour
choices.why: Right. Clustering serves the second filter inside the day.

choices.text: Partition by month, to have fewer pieces
choices.why: Then a one-day question reads a month.

choices.text: Partition by integer range on `items`
choices.why: Nobody filters the rush on the number of items.

prompt: DuckDB's `EXPLAIN ___` runs the query and reports how long each step took, which is how the two layouts were timed.
hint: One word, in capitals in the lesson.

prompt: How many clustering columns may a BigQuery table name?
hint: Fewer than five.

choices.text: One, like the partitioning column
choices.why: Partitioning takes one column; clustering takes more.

choices.text: Up to four
choices.why: Right, and their order matters.

choices.text: Up to sixteen
choices.why: Four is the documented limit.

choices.text: As many as the table has
choices.why: There is a limit, and sorting by every column would sort by none usefully.

prompt: A table is clustered by `store_id, payment`. Which filter skips the fewest blocks?
hint: The second column is sorted only within each value of the first.

choices.text: `store_id = 7 AND payment = 'pix'`
choices.why: Both columns, in order: this skips the most.

choices.text: `store_id = 7`
choices.why: The first column alone skips well.

choices.text: `payment = 'pix'`
choices.why: Right. Pix appears inside every store's run, so it skips little.

choices.text: `store_id IN (7, 8)`
choices.why: Two neighbouring stores still skip most blocks.

prompt: A dry run on a table clustered by `store_id` estimates 2 GiB for a filter on one store, and the query is then billed 0.4 GiB. What happened?
hint: Which skip is known before the query runs?

choices.text: The dry run was wrong and should be reported
choices.why: The estimate is documented as an upper bound for clustered tables.

choices.text: The cache answered part of the query
choices.why: A cached answer bills nothing at all, not part.

choices.text: Blocks were skipped while running, which the dry run cannot see
choices.why: Right. Clustering is the saving found on the bill.

choices.text: Long-term storage halved the bytes
choices.why: Long-term changes a storage rate, never a query's bytes.

prompt: Which of these are true of clustering in BigQuery, by Google's documentation? Choose all that apply.
hint: Think of who pays to keep it sorted.

choices.text: Reclustering runs in the background without using the project's slots
choices.why: Yes, and at no charge.

choices.text: The order of the clustering columns changes which filters skip well
choices.why: Yes, as with a compound sort key.

choices.text: A nightly `VACUUM` has to be scheduled to keep it sorted
choices.why: There is no vacuum; BigQuery does it.

choices.text: Clustering replaces partitioning, so a table has one or the other
choices.why: A table can have both, and Quitanda's does.

prompt: At Quitanda's own size, why did clustering save nothing on the dashboard's bill?
hint: Compare one day of three columns with a threshold.

choices.text: The day's bytes were already under the 10 MB minimum
choices.why: Right. 392,616 bytes is billed as 10,485,760 either way.

choices.text: Clustering only works on `STRING` columns
choices.why: `INT64` is among the documented types.

choices.text: The store asked for was in every row group
choices.why: Only two of nine might hold it.

choices.text: Dashboards are billed by slot-hours
choices.why: On demand bills bytes, whatever the client is.

prompt: A query is billed 0.3058 USD and runs every hour of a 30-day month. What does the month cost, in USD, to two decimal places?
hint: 720 runs.

prompt: Quitanda decides after three years to partition `orders`, which never had partitions. What does the change cost on demand?
hint: BigQuery cannot repartition a table in place.

choices.text: Nothing: `ALTER TABLE` adds partitioning for free
choices.why: Partitioning cannot be added in place.

choices.text: A query reading every byte of every column of the old table, once
choices.why: Right. `CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT *` is billed for all of it.

choices.text: Only the bytes of `dt`
choices.why: Every column has to be read to be written again.

choices.text: The 10 MB minimum
choices.why: Only on a table under 10 MB, which three years of a click stream is not.

prompt: Put the layouts of the dashboard question in order of their bill at a thousand times the size, dearest first.
hint: 220.15, 2.90 and 0.65 USD a month.

prompt: Without partitions, why does the hourly dashboard's bill keep growing while a partitioned one stays flat?
hint: What does each read when the history gets longer?

choices.text: Older partitions cost more to read
choices.why: A byte costs the same whatever its age.

choices.text: It reads every day the table holds, and the history grows; the partitioned one reads one day
choices.why: Right. Partitioning turns a growing cost into a flat one.

choices.text: Long-term storage is added to its query bill
choices.why: Storage and queries are separate bills.

choices.text: The free TiB runs out
choices.why: The free TiB is monthly and the same either way.

prompt: Which of these numbers were measured in this lesson, rather than computed or taken from documentation? Choose all that apply.
hint: DuckDB measured plans, files, row groups and times.

choices.text: A week's filter opened 7 of 60 files
choices.why: Yes, DuckDB's plan.

choices.text: Two of nine row groups might hold store 7
choices.why: Yes, from the files' own statistics.

choices.text: The dashboard costs 0.65 USD a month clustered, at a thousand times
choices.why: Computed, with row groups standing in for blocks.

choices.text: A table may have up to four clustering columns
choices.why: Google's documentation.
